subject: Physics
description: Charge, current, voltage, Ohm's law, power

questions.stem: The SI unit of electric current is the:
questions.explanation: Ampere (A) is the SI base unit of electric current. 1 A = 1 coulomb per second. Volt is the unit of potential difference; ohm is the unit of resistance; coulomb is the unit of charge. The ampere is one of the seven SI base units and was redefined in 2019 in terms of the elementary charge e.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Ohm's law states that in a metallic conductor at constant temperature, the current is:
questions.explanation: Ohm's law: V = IR. At constant temperature, current is directly proportional to voltage, so doubling V doubles I (assuming R is constant). Non-ohmic devices — diodes, filament lamps, thermistors — do not satisfy this relation. Wire resistance itself grows with temperature, which is why long-run steady-state currents in heaters are lower than their cold-start value.

questions.stem: An electrical appliance rated 2 kW is run for 5 hours. The electrical energy consumed is:
questions.explanation: Energy = Power × Time = 2 kW × 5 h = 10 kWh. 1 kWh is the unit a domestic electricity meter measures ('1 unit'). At ₹7/unit this would cost ₹70. A common error is to treat power in W and time in seconds without converting — here 2 kW × 5 h is 10 kWh or 3.6 × 10⁷ J.

questions.stem: The filament of an incandescent bulb is made of which metal?
questions.explanation: Tungsten — extremely high melting point (~3,422 °C) — can glow white-hot without melting. The bulb is filled with inert gas (argon / nitrogen) to slow evaporation of the filament. Copper has a good conductivity but melts at only 1,085 °C. Incandescent bulbs are largely phased out in favour of LEDs because of very poor efficiency (< 5 % of input power becomes light).

questions.stem: The equivalent resistance of two 6 Ω resistors connected in parallel is:
questions.explanation: For two resistors in parallel, R_eq = R₁R₂ / (R₁ + R₂) = 6 × 6 / 12 = 3 Ω. Shortcut — n equal resistors of R each, in parallel, have equivalent R/n. 12 Ω is the series-connection answer (R₁ + R₂), a common trap. In parallel the equivalent resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistor.

questions.stem: A fuse wire is chosen for a circuit because it has:

options.option_text: High melting point and high resistance
Low melting point and high resistance
High melting point and low resistance
Low melting point and low resistance

questions.explanation: A fuse wire must melt quickly when excess current flows — so it needs a low melting point and a high resistance (heat generated is I²R). Common fuse materials are tin-lead alloys. The fuse is always placed in the live wire, never in the neutral, so that on failure the device is isolated from the live supply. Modern installations use MCBs (miniature circuit breakers) that trip instead of melting.

questions.stem: Domestic alternating current supply in India has a standard frequency of:
questions.explanation: India's national grid uses 230 V, 50 Hz AC supply — same as most of Europe and Asia. The USA and Canada use 120 V, 60 Hz. 'Hz' (hertz) means cycles per second — so the voltage reverses direction 100 times per second at 50 Hz. Why AC rather than DC? — easy step-up/step-down via transformers, which makes long-distance transmission efficient.
